ab.title: Aberration: the telescope catches the Earth moving
ab.mini: Every star near the pole of the Earth's orbit swings around a 20″ circle in a year, always displaced toward the direction the Earth is moving: light falling on a moving telescope, as rain on a runner. Bradley found it in 1728.
ab.text: Bradley watched γ Draconis cross his zenith through 1725–1728 and found it swinging back and forth by about 20″ in a year [1]. The displacement points toward the direction in which the Earth is moving at that moment, by κ = v/c, as rain falling on a runner seems to come from ahead. With the light time from the Sun measured from Jupiter's moons, 8 min 12 s, κ = 20.4″ and the orbit's radius follows without any map. Parallax, which also exists, points away from the Sun and is a quarter of a year out of step; for γ Draconis it is a thousand times smaller and drawn here enlarged a thousand times. Earth positions from an ephemeris [2]; the orbit is not to scale, the star's offsets are to their 10″ bar.
ab.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: no yearly swing common to all stars, or a swing that follows the Sun's direction rather than the Earth's velocity.
sun.title: The Sun is 3.4 % wider in January than in July
sun.mini: Through 2023 SDO's apparent radius of the Sun runs from 976″ in early January to 944″ in early July and back: the Earth is 5 million km closer to the Sun in January. The orbit is drawn to scale.
sun.text: The Sun's apparent radius, as SDO measured it every seven days of 2023 [1], next to the Earth on its orbit drawn to scale, eccentricity 0.017, with its distance from an ephemeris [2]. The disc is drawn at the measured radius between the year's largest, early January, and smallest, early July. The ratio of the two, 1.034, is (1 + e)/(1 − e). SDO's radius is computed by its pipeline from the spacecraft's distance, so this is a check; a camera with a fixed lens and a solar filter measures the same ratio in pixels. A lamp circling above a plane would change size by a large factor within each day.
sun.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun's apparent size changing within a day, between noon and sunset, rather than over a year.
dop.title: The Sun's Doppler shift follows the ground through the day
dop.mini: In the morning La Palma is carried toward the Sun and sees it approach; in the afternoon away, and sees it recede. HARPS-N records exactly the globe's curve, with no shape fitted; the best flat lamp misses it.
dop.text: The Earth seen from above the North Pole, with La Palma carried around on its parallel and the Sun far to the right. Its velocity, about 400 m/s, points partly toward the Sun in the morning and partly away from it in the afternoon. The HARPS-N solar telescope on La Palma records the Sun's velocity every five minutes [1]: the measured day, its timestamp named above the text, follows the globe's curve, Ω R cos φ cos δ sin H with R = 6,371 km and the Sun placed by an ephemeris [2], with no shape fitted. The flat model's lamp, its height fitted over 462 days in its favour, departs from it in the morning and the afternoon. The Earth and the Sun are not to scale.
dop.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a lamp height that fits the solar velocities as closely as the globe's curve, about 1 m/s.
star.title: A star seems to approach and recede once a year
star.mini: τ Ceti's observed velocity swings by ±27 km/s every year. The curve drawn from the Earth's orbit alone, at 29.8 km/s, follows 561 HARPS nights with only the star's own mean velocity adjusted.
star.text: τ Ceti barely moves; the observer does. HARPS measured its velocity on 561 nights from 2003 to 2019 [1]; folded on one year they swing by ±27 km/s. The Earth, moving at 29.8 km/s along its orbit, comes toward τ Ceti for half the year and goes away for the other half; the part of its speed directed at the star, cos β with β the star's angle from the orbit's plane, is the swing. The curve drawn is computed from the Earth's position alone, from an ephemeris [2], with only the star's own mean velocity, −16.1 km/s, adjusted. The orbit is not to scale.
star.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: stellar velocities with no yearly swing, or a swing of the same size for stars at every angle from the orbit's plane.
par.title: A near star shifts against the far ones
par.mini: 61 Cygni moves around a small ellipse, 0.314″ across each way, against fainter stars behind it, always on the side opposite the Earth. Bessel measured it in 1838: the first distance to a star.
par.text: Bessel measured 61 Cygni against fainter, more distant stars through 1837–1838 and found it moving around a small ellipse of half-width 0.314″ [1]: the near star seen from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. Its shift points away from the Earth's position, here from an ephemeris [2], so it is a quarter of a year out of step with aberration, which moves the whole field by about 20″ and is removed here, as is the star's own drift of 5.2″ a year. The triangle whose base is the orbit puts 61 Cygni about 660,000 times further than the Sun. The orbit and the star are not to scale; the shifts are to their 0.2″ bar.
par.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: near stars that do not shift against far ones over a year, or shifts that are the same for every star whatever its distance.
kep.title: Kepler's three laws of orbits
kep.mini: A planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, sweeps equal areas in equal times, and an orbit four times wider takes eight times longer. Kepler read the three laws in Tycho Brahe's observations; Newton showed they all come from one force.
kep.text: Kepler found three rules in Tycho Brahe's observations of the planets [1]. Each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet goes fastest when it is nearest. The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's size, with one constant for every planet: an orbit four times wider takes eight times longer, since 4³ = 8². Newton showed that all three follow from a single attraction toward the Sun that weakens as the inverse square of the distance, and that the constant of the third law is 4π²/GM, set by the mass of the body at the centre alone [2]. The same law, with the Earth's much smaller GM, governs the Moon and every satellite. The ellipse drawn here is far more eccentric than the Earth's orbit (0.6 against 0.017); the two circles on the right are to scale between them. The band under the drawing gives the three laws with the values of the moment shown: r from the ellipse's equation, ½r²θ̇ constant at 0.400, and (8T)²/(4a)³ = T²/a³.
kep.verdict: Would favour the flat model: bodies circling the Earth whose periods and distances do not follow T² ∝ a³ with one and the same constant.
fall.title: How a falling body can orbit
fall.mini: In its first second anything falls 4.9 m. Sideways at 7.9 km/s, the ground curves away by 4.9 m over the 7.9 km covered: the ball falls, but never gets closer to the ground. That is an orbit.
fall.text: Newton's thought experiment [1]: a cannon on a very high mountain fires balls sideways, faster and faster. Each falls under gravity; the slower ones land, farther each time. Near the ground everything falls 4.9 m in its first second, whatever its sideways speed, and over 7.9 km the Earth's surface curves down by (7.9 km)²/2R = 4.9 m. So a ball moving sideways at 7.9 km/s has fallen 4.9 m in that second while the ground beneath it has fallen away by the same 4.9 m: it keeps its height, second after second, and goes all the way round, in 84 minutes without air. Falling and orbiting are the same motion; the speed v = √(gR) is what makes the fall follow the curve of the ground. The right half of the animation is at true scale: the first 200 seconds of an orbit 30 km up, the drop below a straight line equal to the ground's. The mountain on the left is not to scale. The band under the drawing gives the equations with the values of the moment shown: v²/r against GM/r², ½gt² against (vt)²/2R, v = √(gR) and the period 2π√(R/g).
fall.verdict: Would favour the flat model: a body thrown sideways at 7.9 km/s that comes down like a slower one, because a flat ground does not curve away beneath it.
cannon.title: Newton's cannon at 400 km: from a dropped ball to an orbit
cannon.mini: A cannon 400 km up fires level, harder each time. At 0.34 m/s the ball lands 100 m away; at 3.1 km/s, 1,000 km away; at 7.53 km/s, 15,000 km away. At 7.67 km/s it never lands: it falls all the way round the Earth, one turn in 92 minutes.
cannon.text: Newton's thought experiment [1], with numbers. A cannon held 400 km above the ground fires level; the only pull is the Earth's, taken from the orbit of the GPS satellites [2]. Dropped without speed, the ball takes five minutes to reach the ground. Fired at 0.34 m/s it lands 100 m from the foot of the cannon, at 339 m/s 100 km away, at 3.1 km/s 1,000 km away, at 7.0 km/s 5,000 km away and at 7.53 km/s 15,000 km away: each time the ground has curved away a little more under it. Past 7.55 km/s it misses the ground altogether, and at 7.67 km/s it keeps its height: a circle, one turn in 92.4 minutes, which is what the International Space Station does at that height [3]. The camera follows the ball; the small frame shows the whole Earth. True scale; no air and no rotation of the Earth in the calculation.
cannon.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: over a plane with the same pull everywhere, the ball lands after 4 min 45 s whatever its speed, so nothing fired level could stay up. A satellite whose period did not follow from its height would count against the globe.
radar.title: A radar clock measures the Sun's distance
radar.mini: In 1961 the Millstone radar timed 25 echoes from Venus: 283 to 449 seconds there and back, so Venus was 42 to 67 million km away. Reduced with today's orbits, the echoes give an astronomical unit of 149,597,863 km.
radar.text: From March to May 1961 the Millstone radar sent pulses to Venus and timed the echoes to a ten-thousandth of a second: 283 to 449 seconds there and back [1]. The orbits give the Earth–Venus distance in astronomical units; the echo gives it in kilometres. Reduced again with today's orbits (DE440) [2], the 25 echoes give 149,597,863 km (median), within 193 km of one another and 8 km of today's value; the 1962 reduction with Newcomb's orbits drifted by 2,000 km.
radar.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: echoes from Venus coming back in a fraction of a second, or flight times that no single astronomical unit fits from March to May.
psr.title: Pulsar clocks feel the Earth going round the Sun
psr.mini: Millisecond pulsars' pulses arrive up to 499 seconds early or late through the year, by A·cos β/c. Timing gives the product; quasar-referenced positions give β. Twelve pulsars, two arrays: A = 149,597,870.7 km.
psr.text: The pulses of a millisecond pulsar come early when the Earth is on the pulsar's side of its orbit and late on the other side, by up to (A/c)·cos β, β the pulsar's latitude above the orbit. Timing alone fixes only A·cos β [1]; the latitude measured against quasars by interferometry splits the product [2]. For twelve pulsars timed by EPTA and NANOGrav, A = 149,597,870.7 km (median of twenty timing models), each within its error.
psr.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: pulsars whose pulses show no annual delay, or delays whose sizes do not follow cos β.
transit.title: Transits of Venus, 1761, 1769, 2012: timed around the world
transit.mini: Venus touched the Sun's edge minutes apart for observers at Tahiti, Vardø, California or Hudson Bay: the Earth's size seen from the Sun. 1769, 228 timings: 149.6 ± 1.9 million km; 1761: 153 ± 4; 2012 (amateurs, one contact): 159 ± 3.
transit.text: Seen from places thousands of kilometres apart, the same contact of Venus with the Sun's edge comes minutes apart, by an amount set by the Earth's size against the Sun's distance (Halley's method). Newcomb's collection of every timing of 1761 and 1769 [1], and the amateurs' timings of 2012, each contact computed again for each station with today's orbits [2]: 1769 gives 149.57 ± 1.89 million km, 1761 153.0 ± 3.9, 2012 158.8 ± 2.5 from one contact alone (the project's own value); the three together 151.0 ± 1.8.
transit.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: contact times that do not depend on where they were taken, or that depend on it far more than a Sun at 150 million km allows.
